draft.title: Land clearing and erosion
card: Ground cover is the layer of plants, leaves and roots that covers soil. It slows rain, and roots hold soil in place.
Clearing forests for farms or palm oil plantations removes this cover. Heavy use of a walking track can wear it away too, as boots trample the plants.
Bare soil is easily eroded. Erosion is the wearing away and movement of soil by water or wind. Rain splashes soil loose and runoff carries it downhill.
Eroded soil can wash into rivers. This makes the water muddy and can settle on the riverbed. The land that lost its topsoil is also left less fertile.
draft.remember: Less ground cover means more soil washed away, often into rivers.

a.q: Why does clearing a hillside forest make soil erosion more likely?
opts: Bare soil has no plants or roots to hold it against rain
The soil becomes heavier, so it slides down the hill
Rain falls harder on land that has no trees
Farm crops always have shallower roots than trees
a.why: Trees, leaves and roots protect soil and hold it in place. Without them, rain and runoff can carry soil away. Rain does not fall harder on cleared land, it is only that the soil is no longer protected.
a.clue: Think about what the plants were doing for the soil.

b.q: A popular walking track in Tasmania has been used by thousands of hikers. Plants beside it have died, and after rain the path has deep gullies. What is the best explanation?
opts: Trampling removed ground cover, so rain carried soil away
Hikers carried soil away on their boots, leaving gullies
Rain caused the plants to die, so the soil moved
The gullies formed because the soil had too many roots
b.why: Many boots wear away the plants that cover the soil. With the cover gone, rain runoff easily washes soil down the track. Soil on boots is a tiny amount compared with what runoff moves.
b.clue: What happens to plants when many people walk on them?

a.best: Bare soil has no plants or roots to hold it against rain

b.best: Trampling removed ground cover, so rain carried soil away

problems.detail: The card says ground cover 'slows rain', so a student could fairly infer that rain hits bare, cleared land harder. This makes the distractor 'Rain falls harder on land that has no trees' look half-right. Rewording it so it is plainly false would avoid the clash, for example 'Rain falls more often on land that has no trees'.
